title: A smooth dense open after a finite radicial base change
statement:
Let $S$ be integral of finite type over a field and let
$X\to S$ be of finite type with $X\ne\varnothing$.
After shrinking $S$, there is a finite radicial surjection
$S'\to S$ such that $(X_{S'})_{\mathrm{red}}$ has a dense
open $V$ smooth over $S'$. For a constructible finite sheaf
$F$ on $X$, one may require its pullback to $V$ to be
locally constant. Every component of the complement in the
generic fiber then has dimension strictly smaller than the
dimension of the component of $X_{S'}$ that contains it.
The notation refers to scheme conventions.

proof.text: Apply [lem-pur-generic-geometrically-reduced-preparation] to $X\to S$. Replace $S$ by the resulting nonempty $U$ and put $Y=(X\times_S S\prime)_{\mathrm{red}}$. Thus $S\prime$ is integral affine, $q$ is finite and a universal homeomorphism, $g:Y\to S\prime$ is flat of finite presentation, and $Y_{\eta\prime}$ is geometrically reduced. By the definition of universal homeomorphism every base change of $q$ is bijective on points. Consequently $q$ is surjective and universally injective, hence radicial by [def-weil-radicial-morphism]. This establishes precisely the required base change, without imposing geometric irreducibility on any fibre.

On the generic fibre apply [lem-pur-geometrically-reduced-dense-smooth-open]. Every smooth generic-fibre point has an open neighbourhood in $Y$ smooth over $S\prime$: in affine charts $\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}A$, apply [lem-weil-pbc-flat-smooth-fibre-smooth-at-prime] to the corresponding prime $\mathfrak q$. Its three hypotheses hold: $B$ is finitely presented over $A$ (take the localization element $1$), the local map is flat because $g$ is flat, and the corresponding fibre prime is smooth by our choice of point. The conclusion, unpacked by [def-weil-pbc-singular-ideal], gives $b\notin\mathfrak q$ with $B_b$ smooth over $A$. These open charts have union $V_0$, smooth by the affine-local characterization in [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms]. Its generic fibre contains the dense smooth locus. It is dense in all of $Y$: for every nonempty open $O\subseteq Y$, openness of $g$ from [lem-weil-pbc-flat-lfp-open] implies $g(O)$ is a nonempty open of integral $S\prime$, hence contains $\eta\prime$. Therefore $O_{\eta\prime}$ is nonempty and meets $(V_0)_{\eta\prime}$.

The spaces in use are Noetherian. Indeed $S$ is finite type over a field, $S\prime$ is finite over an open of $S$, and $Y$ is finite type over $S\prime$. On a finite affine covering the coordinate algebras are finite type over a field and Noetherian by [lem-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra-noetherian] (a field has only the ideals $0$ and $1$). For a Noetherian ring $B$, an ascending chain of ideals stabilizes: its union is an ideal with finitely many generators, all lying in one member of the chain. A descending chain of closed subsets of $\operatorname{Spec}B$ corresponds to an ascending chain of radical ideals, so stabilizes. Thus each affine chart is a Noetherian space. A finite union of Noetherian open subspaces is Noetherian: an ascending chain of opens stabilizes on each chart and hence globally. In particular $Y$ has finitely many irreducible components by [lem-weil-pbc-noetherian-finite-components].

proof.text: For the sheaf assertion pull back $F$ to $Y$; it is constructible by [prop-constructible-pullback]. Choose its finite locally closed stratification from [def-constructible-constructible]. Let $W$ be the union of the interiors of its underlying strata in $Y$. This union contains every generic point $\xi$ of $Y$: if a stratum is $O\cap C$ with $O$ open and $C$ closed and contains $\xi$, it contains $O\cap\overline{\{\xi\}}$; removing the finitely many other components gives an open neighbourhood of $\xi$ contained in this stratum. Thus $W$ is dense. On an interior $W_i$, the base change of its stratum immersion is a surjective immersion $Z_i\times_YW_i\to W_i$. It is a closed immersion locally on $W_i$ (an immersion with entire underlying image), and its defining ideal is contained in every prime, so its elements are nilpotent. After any ring base change the image ideal still consists of nilpotents: a finite sum of nilpotent commuting elements is nilpotent. Its spectrum map is therefore a homeomorphism after every base change, so this is a universal homeomorphism. The pullback of $F|_{W_i}$ to this stratum is locally constant by [lemma-constructible-pullback-locally-constant]. By [lemma-constructible-universal-homeomorphism-invariance] $F|_{W_i}$ is locally constant as well. These restrictions supply local trivializations on their union $W$. Set $V=V_0\cap W$. It remains smooth and is dense, since both opens contain all generic points. Without $F$, take $V=V_0$.

proof.text: Finally let $Z$ be any irreducible component of the generic-fibre complement $Y_{\eta\prime}\setminus V_{\eta\prime}$, and let $C$ be an irreducible component of $Y$ containing it. The closure $\overline Z$ in $Y$ is irreducible, is contained in $C\cap(Y\setminus V)$, and is a proper closed subset of $C$ because $V$ contains the generic point of $C$. The dimension of $Y$ is finite by [lem-kun-dimension-finite-type], since $Y$ is finite type over the original field. Write $d=\dim C$. Apply [new-node-irreducible-open-complement-dimension] to $C$ and its nonempty open $C\cap V$. The complement $C\setminus V$ is nonempty because it contains the nonempty $Z$. Hence the nonempty-complement clause gives an integer $e<d$ with $\dim(C\setminus V)\leq e$, and in particular $\dim(C\setminus V)<d$. The generic fibre has the subspace topology in $Y$ by [def-pc-scheme-fibre]. Every strict chain of irreducible closed subsets in $Z$ gives a strict chain of their closures in $C\setminus V$: closure intersected back with the subspace $Z$ is the original closed subset, which preserves strictness. Therefore $\dim Z\leq\dim(C\setminus V)<\dim C$. Reduction has the same underlying space as $X_{S\prime}$, so this is the stated comparison. If the generic fibre or complement is empty the assertion is vacuous, and $V=\varnothing$ is allowed when shrinking removes all of $X$.
